prompt: True or False: Client-side validation is enough to secure your app — if the form rejects bad input, no bad data reaches your server.

config.statement: Client-side validation is enough to secure your app — if the form rejects bad input, no bad data reaches your server.

hints: Can someone bypass your JavaScript and send an HTTP request directly?
Think about tools like Postman or curl
explanation: False. Client-side validation is only for user experience. Anyone can bypass it by using curl, Postman, or browser dev tools to send a direct HTTP request to your server. Always validate *again* on the server before processing or storing data. Client-side = convenience, server-side = security.

prompt: True or false: a page missing <!DOCTYPE html> and <html lang="en"> will fail to display anything in the browser.

config.statement: A page missing <!DOCTYPE html> and lang="en" fails to display at all.
config.rubric: A full answer says false and explains the page still renders, but loses things like standards-mode rendering and correct screen-reader pronunciation.

hints: Browsers are built to be forgiving of missing structure, not to refuse to render.
Think about what specifically DOCTYPE and lang actually control, rather than whether the page 'works' at all.
explanation: False. The page will still render — browsers fill in missing structure silently rather than refusing to show anything. What's actually lost is more subtle: without DOCTYPE, the browser may use an old backwards-compatibility rendering mode with different sizing rules; without lang="en", a screen reader has no reliable signal for which language's pronunciation to use. Nothing crashes, but real things quietly degrade.

prompt: Match each page region to the semantic element that correctly describes its role.

pairs.left: The page's actual main content, distinct from repeated boilerplate
A self-contained blog post that could stand alone
The page's top banner with logo and title

hints: Ask what each region actually is, not what it looks like once styled.
<div> is the fallback for when none of the semantic options honestly fit — check whether one of them does first.
explanation: <nav> for navigation links, <main> for the page's actual content (only one per page), <article> for self-contained, independently distributable content like a blog post, <header> for the top banner region. <div> and <section> are both real elements, but neither is the best fit here: <div> carries no meaning at all, and <section> is for a themed grouping that isn't independently distributable the way an <article> is.

prompt: True or false: using <div> to wrap a section purely so you can apply a background color with CSS, with no other role, is a mistake you should always fix by finding a semantic tag instead.

config.statement: A <div> used only to apply CSS styling, with no independent semantic role, should always be replaced with a semantic tag.
config.rubric: A full answer says false and explains that div/span are the correct, honest choice when a wrapper genuinely has no semantic role of its own.

hints: The rule from this lesson is 'use div/span when there genuinely is no semantic role' — not 'never use div.'
Forcing a semantic tag onto something that isn't actually that thing is its own kind of inaccurate.
explanation: False. When a wrapper's only job is applying CSS, with no independent meaning to announce, <div> (or <span> for inline content) is the honest, correct choice — not a shortcut to be eliminated. Reaching for a semantic tag that doesn't actually describe the region's role (calling a purely decorative wrapper a <section>, say) is its own kind of wrong. The rule is "pick the tag that matches the real role," and sometimes the real role genuinely is "none, this is just styling."

prompt: A photo shows a red, slightly swollen rash on a forearm, used on a symptom-tracking page so the patient can compare it day to day. Which alt text is actually useful?

options.text: alt="image"
alt="rash.jpg"
alt="Red, slightly swollen rash on the inner forearm, roughly 3cm across"
alt="image of a rash on someone's arm"

hints: Write it like you're describing the photo to someone on the phone who can't see it.
"image of..." is redundant — screen readers already announce that it's an image before reading the alt text.
explanation: "Red, slightly swollen rash on the inner forearm, roughly 3cm across" — specific enough to actually be useful for comparing day to day, without needing to see the photo. "image" and the file name convey nothing. "image of a rash on someone's arm" is closer, but the word "image" is redundant (already announced by the screen reader) and it's less specific than it could be about size, location, and appearance — exactly the details that would matter for tracking a symptom.

prompt: Sort each image by whether it should get a real, descriptive alt text or an empty alt="".

items.text: A photo documenting a visible symptom
A purely decorative border graphic between sections
An icon that's actually a clickable "delete entry" button

hints: Ask: if this image were deleted, would the page lose any actual information?
A functional image (one that's really a button) gets alt text describing the action, which still counts as 'real, descriptive.'
explanation: Documenting a symptom and a functional delete button both carry real information (a symptom's appearance; what clicking will do) and need real alt text. A decorative border and a repeated background pattern carry no information of their own — deleting them loses nothing — so alt="" is correct, telling screen readers to skip them rather than announce noise.

prompt: Which of these correctly connects a label to its input, so clicking the label text also focuses the field and a screen reader announces the label when the field is focused?

options.text: <label>Dose (mg)</label><input type="number">
<label for="dose">Dose (mg)</label><input type="number" id="dose">
<input type="number" placeholder="Dose (mg)">
<label for="doseAmount">Dose (mg)</label><input type="number" id="dose">

hints: The label's `for` attribute and the input's `id` attribute have to match exactly, character for character.
A label with no `for`, or an input with no matching `id`, isn't connected to anything — it's just nearby text.
explanation: <label for="dose">Dose (mg)</label><input type="number" id="dose"> — the for and id values match exactly ("dose"), which is what creates the actual connection. The first option has a label and input that are visually adjacent but not programmatically linked at all. The third uses only a placeholder, which vanishes on focus. The fourth has mismatched values ("doseAmount" vs "dose") — close, but a mismatch is the same as no connection at all.

prompt: You're building a form field for someone's phone number, and another for how many hours they slept last night (a number 0-24). For each, name the specific input type you'd use instead of a generic type="text", and explain what real benefit it gives someone filling out the form on a phone.
hints: Think about what keyboard shows up on a phone for each type, and whether the browser can catch an invalid value before submission.
type="tel" and type="number" both exist for reasons more concrete than just labeling — what do they actually change?
explanation: Phone number: type="tel" — brings up the numeric phone keypad on mobile instead of the full keyboard, faster and less error-prone to use one-handed. Hours slept: type="number" — also brings up a numeric keypad, and lets the browser reject a non-numeric entry (or one outside a set min/max) before the form is even submitted, catching a mistake immediately rather than after a round trip. Both would technically still accept valid input as type="text", but they throw away the better keyboard and built-in validation the specific types give for free.

prompt: True or false: counts as having proper alt text, since the alt attribute is present and non-empty.

config.statement: alt="chart.png" is proper alt text because the attribute is present and not empty.
config.rubric: A full answer says false and explains that repeating the file name conveys no more information than no alt text at all.

hints: Being present isn't the same as being useful — does this alt text tell you anything the file name wouldn't?
This is functionally identical to the no-alt fallback behavior — it just typed the file name manually instead of letting the browser guess it.
explanation: False. Technically the attribute is present, but repeating the file name conveys nothing about what the chart actually shows — it's no more useful than the file-name fallback a screen reader would use if the attribute were missing entirely. Real alt text has to describe the content: what the chart shows, not what the file is named.

prompt: <input type="checkbox"> Took meds today — with no label at all, just that text sitting next to the checkbox. What's the actual risk, beyond looking slightly off?

options.text: A screen reader announces the checkbox with no indication of what it's asking
The checkbox will fail to submit with the form
The text next to it is automatically read as its label by every browser
There's no real risk — visual proximity is enough

hints: Text sitting next to an input isn't the same as text programmatically connected to it.
A screen reader relies on a real <label> (or aria-label) connection, not visual layout, to know what a field is asking.
explanation: Without a real <label> (or equivalent), a screen reader announces "checkbox, not checked" with nothing about what it's for — visual proximity means nothing to assistive technology, which reads the underlying structure, not the layout. The fix: <label><input type="checkbox"> Took meds today</label>, or a label with a matching for/id.

prompt: Sort each link's text by whether it's genuinely descriptive out of context, or meaningless if a screen reader user hears it isolated in a list of every link on the page.
hints: Imagine hearing only the link text, with none of the surrounding sentence — does it say where it goes?
"Click here" and "Read more" could be the text of literally any link on any page.
explanation: "Click here" and "Read more" say nothing about the destination — heard alone, out of context, they're interchangeable with any other link on the internet. "View today's symptom log" and "Download your March medication report (PDF)" describe exactly where the link goes, which is what a screen reader user scanning a page's link list actually needs.

prompt: A page's entire visible content — header, three articles, and a footer — is written as five sibling <div>s with no other tags. Visually it's a complete, well-designed page. Structurally, what does it actually communicate?

options.text: The full layout, exactly as intended, to both sighted users and screen readers
Five generic groups, indistinguishable from each other, to anything not reading the visual layout
An error, since a page can't be built entirely from divs
The same information, just formatted slightly differently

hints: A <div> carries no built-in meaning at all, regardless of how many of them there are or how they're arranged.
What a screen reader announces depends on tag names, not on visual layout or arrangement.
explanation: Five sibling <div>s are five identical, meaningless groups as far as a screen reader is concerned — no signal for header, article, or footer at all, even though the visual result can be pixel-perfect. Swapping in <header>, three <article>s, and <footer> would look identical while actually communicating the page's real structure.

prompt: A "Submit" button sits at the bottom of three different forms on a site: a newsletter signup, a symptom log, and an account deletion. What's the real problem with all three sharing the same label?

options.text: There's no problem — Submit is a standard, universally understood label
Out of context (like a list of every button on the page), "Submit" gives no clue which of three very different actions it triggers
Submit buttons need to be a different color on each form
Forms can only have one Submit button per page, total

hints: Think about how a screen reader user might browse a page's buttons out of context, the same way link text was covered earlier.
One of these three actions is a lot higher-stakes than the other two — does the label reflect that at all?
explanation: Heard out of context — which is a real way screen reader users scan a page — "Submit" gives zero indication whether pressing it signs you up for a newsletter, logs a symptom, or deletes an account entirely. Specific labels ("Subscribe", "Save entry", "Permanently delete account") describe the actual, very different consequences of each button.

prompt: You want to style just the single element with id="pageHeader", and nothing else, even if other elements share its tag or class. Which selector is correct?

options.text: header { }
.pageHeader { }
#pageHeader { }

hints: An id selector uses a hash (#), and ids are meant to be unique to one element on the page.
A class selector (.pageHeader) could match multiple elements if the class is reused — an id can't.
explanation: #pageHeader targets the one element with id="pageHeader", and only that element — ids are meant to be unique per page. header would match every <header> element on the page; .pageHeader would match every element carrying that class, even if reused elsewhere; * matches literally everything.

prompt: True or false: if #summary { color: blue; } is written before .summary { color: green; } in the same stylesheet, the text ends up green, because the later rule always wins.

config.statement: The later-written rule always wins, regardless of selector type.
config.rubric: A full answer says false and explains that id selectors are more specific than class selectors, so the id rule wins regardless of order.

hints: Write order only decides the winner when specificity is exactly tied.
An id selector (#) is higher specificity than a class selector (.), full stop.
explanation: False. #summary is an id selector, which has higher specificity than a class selector like .summary — the id rule wins regardless of which was written first or last. Write order is only the tiebreaker when two rules have equal specificity, which isn't the case here.

prompt: Order these box model layers from innermost (closest to the text) to outermost.
hints: The text itself is the innermost layer — everything else wraps around it.
Margin is always the outermost, invisible layer — it pushes neighboring elements away.
explanation: Content, Padding, Border, Margin — innermost to outermost. The text/content sits at the center, padding wraps it (and shares its background), border draws a visible line around the padding, and margin is invisible space outside the border, separating this box from its neighbors.

prompt: A box has box-sizing: border-box, width: 200px, padding: 20px, and a 2px border. How wide does it actually render?

options.text: 200px — width now means the total rendered width, including padding and border
244px — padding and border are still added on top
156px — padding and border are subtracted twice
It depends on the browser

hints: This is exactly what border-box changes from the default — reread what the property is named after.
With border-box, the content area shrinks to make room for padding and border, rather than the whole box growing.
explanation: 200px. box-sizing: border-box redefines width to mean the total rendered box — content, padding and border all fit inside that 200px, with the content area shrinking to make room, rather than padding and border being added on top the way they are with the default content-box sizing.

prompt:
You have
and want the three buttons spaced evenly with room pushed to both edges. Which rule, added to .row along with display: flex, does that?

options.text: justify-content: space-between;
align-items: center;
flex-direction: column;

hints: justify-content controls spacing along the row; align-items controls alignment across the row's height instead.
space-between pushes the first and last items to the edges and evenly distributes space between the rest.
explanation: justify-content: space-between — pushes the first and last flex items to the container's edges, with even space distributed between the items in the middle. align-items controls the perpendicular axis (vertical alignment in a row), not horizontal spacing. flex-direction: column would stack them vertically instead. gap adds fixed space, not evenly distributed edge-to-edge spacing.

prompt: True or false: with the default flex-wrap value (nowrap), flex items that don't fit on one line will automatically move to a second line.

config.statement: By default, flex items that don't fit will wrap onto a second line automatically.
config.rubric: A full answer says false and explains that the default is nowrap, which squeezes or overflows items instead of wrapping them.

hints: The default value's name is literally 'nowrap' — what would that imply about its behavior?
You have to explicitly set flex-wrap: wrap to get the wrapping behavior.
explanation: False. The default is flex-wrap: nowrap, which tries to keep every item on a single line — squeezing them thinner if they don't fit, or letting the row overflow its container. Wrapping onto a second line only happens once you explicitly set flex-wrap: wrap.

prompt: A designer proposes light gray text (which measures 2.8:1 contrast) on a white background for a page's body copy. Does this meet WCAG AA for normal-sized text?

options.text: Yes — it's close enough to look fine
No — normal text needs at least 4.5:1, and 2.8:1 falls well short
Yes — any contrast ratio above 2:1 passes
It depends entirely on the font used

hints: The WCAG AA minimum for normal-sized text is a specific number — 4.5:1.
"Close enough" isn't how a hard minimum works — 2.8:1 is meaningfully below 4.5:1, not a rounding difference.
explanation: No. WCAG AA requires at least 4.5:1 for normal-sized text; 2.8:1 falls well short, not just marginally. This pairing would need a darker gray (or black) to pass, regardless of font choice — font affects readability at a given contrast, but doesn't change the measured ratio itself.

prompt: Sort each design choice by whether it uses color as the only signal, or pairs it with something else.

categories: Color is paired with a non-color signal

items.text: A required field marked only by turning its label red
An error field with a red border plus the text "Required" below it
items.category: Color is paired with a non-color signal

items.text: A chart distinguishing three categories only by line color
A status dot that's green or red, plus the word "Online"/"Offline" next to it
items.category: Color is paired with a non-color signal

hints: Ask: if you removed all color and left everything else, would the meaning survive?
Text labels, icons, and patterns all count as non-color signals.
explanation: A red label alone and a chart distinguished only by line color both fail the "remove color" test — nothing else conveys the meaning. The bordered field with "Required" text and the status dot with a text label both survive, because the actual information (required, online/offline) is also stated directly, not just implied by color.

prompt: A page's main content area is set to width: 900px. On a 375px-wide phone screen, what's the correct fix to prevent horizontal overflow while still allowing up to 900px on wide screens?

options.text: Change to max-width: 900px; width: 100%;
Change to width: 375px;
Delete the width rule entirely and add nothing in its place
Add display: flex; with no other change

hints: A fixed number, even a smaller one, is still fixed — it'll be wrong for some other screen size.
max-width sets a ceiling that a relative width (100%) can shrink below on a narrower screen.
explanation: max-width: 900px; width: 100%; grows up to 900px on a wide screen but shrinks to fit 100% of the available space on a narrower one — genuinely responsive. width: 375px just swaps one fixed, wrong-for-most-screens number for another. Removing the rule entirely leaves the default block behavior, which is closer but loses the intentional max width on large screens. display: flex changes nothing about the width itself.

prompt: You want a two-column layout (sidebar + main content, side by side) on a laptop screen, but stacked vertically (sidebar above main content) on any screen 600px wide or narrower. Describe the CSS approach — the base layout, and what the media query changes.
hints: Start with the flexbox row as your normal, unconditional layout — that's the default for wide screens.
The media query only needs to override flex-direction; everything else about the flex container can stay the same.
explanation: Base rule: a parent container with display: flex; (default flex-direction: row) holding the sidebar and main content side by side — this is the layout for anything wider than 600px. Then: @media (max-width: 600px) { .container { flex-direction: column; } } — below 600px, the same flex container switches to stacking its children vertically instead of horizontally. No second page or duplicated markup is needed; the same HTML just gets a different flex-direction depending on screen width.

prompt: You want every button on the page styled the same way, and there are 12 of them, none needing individual styling. Which selector is the right fit?

options.text: button { }
#button { } repeated 12 times with different ids
.button1, .button2, .button3 { } (one class per button)

hints: When every element of a tag should share the same style, the plain element selector is usually the simplest correct choice.
Ids are meant to be unique — repeating #button 12 times with different names is a sign the wrong tool is being reached for.
explanation: button { } matches every <button> on the page in one rule — exactly right when there's no need to differentiate them. Twelve unique ids or twelve separate classes would both work but add repetition with no benefit, since none of the buttons actually need individual treatment.

prompt: A card's background color only fills a small area around the text, even though you set padding: 40px. What's the most likely explanation?

options.text: The padding value is actually being applied as margin instead, by a typo or misunderstanding
Padding never affects background color
40px is too small a number to have any visible effect
Background colors ignore padding by design

hints: Padding is inside the border and does pick up the background color — margin is outside and never does.
If the background looks tight to the text despite a large padding value, check whether margin was written instead.
explanation: Padding fills with the box's background color; margin never does, since it's outside the border. If a large padding value isn't visibly expanding the colored area, the most likely cause is that margin was set instead (or in addition), which pushes the box away from neighbors but does nothing to the colored area itself.

prompt: Three flex items need to sit in a horizontal row, centered together as a group in the middle of their container (not spread to the edges). Which value of justify-content does that?

options.text: center
space-between
flex-start
stretch

hints: space-between pushes items to the edges — the opposite of grouping them together in the middle.
stretch is an align-items value for the perpendicular axis, not a justify-content value.
explanation: justify-content: center groups the flex items together and centers that group within the container. space-between spreads them to the edges with gaps between (the opposite effect). flex-start packs them to the start of the row. stretch isn't even a valid justify-content value in most cases — it's typically used with align-items instead.

prompt: True or false: a light blue button with white text that measures 2.1:1 contrast is fine as long as the button also has a visible border, since the border makes it obvious there's a button there.

config.statement: Low text contrast on a button is acceptable as long as the button shape/border is still visible.
config.rubric: A full answer says false and explains that a visible border tells you a button exists, but doesn't help anyone actually read its label text.

hints: Being able to see that something is a button and being able to read what it says are two separate problems.
The contrast requirement is specifically about the text itself, not the element's outline.
explanation: False. A visible border solves a different problem (locating the button) than text contrast solves (reading its label). At 2.1:1, well under the 4.5:1 minimum, the button's text itself is hard to read regardless of how clearly its edges are visible — someone can see there's a button there and still not be able to make out what it says.

prompt: Put these CSS box-sizing debugging steps in the order you'd actually do them, from noticing the problem to confirming the fix.

items: Notice the box is rendering wider than the width value you set
Check whether padding or border is being added on top (default content-box)
Add box-sizing: border-box to the element (or globally)
Confirm the box now renders at exactly the width you specified

hints: You have to notice the symptom before you can diagnose the cause.
The fix (border-box) only makes sense once you've confirmed padding/border is the actual cause.
explanation: Notice the mismatch, diagnose it (default content-box adds padding/border on top of width), apply the fix (box-sizing: border-box), then confirm the box now matches the intended size. Skipping the diagnosis step and jumping straight to "add border-box everywhere" usually still works, but understanding why is what lets you actually predict box sizes going forward.

prompt: A row of five tags overflows off the right edge of a narrow phone screen. The container already has display: flex;. What single addition most directly fixes the overflow?

options.text: flex-wrap: wrap;
justify-content: center;
color: red;
font-weight: bold;

hints: The default flex-wrap (nowrap) tries to keep everything on one line, which is exactly what causes overflow when there isn't room.
Centering the row doesn't create more room — it just shifts where the overflow happens.
explanation: flex-wrap: wrap directly fixes the overflow by letting extra tags flow onto additional lines instead of forcing them all onto one. justify-content: center would just recenter an overflowing row, not fix the overflow itself. Color and font-weight have no effect on layout at all.

prompt: A page looks perfect at your laptop's window width. A friend opens it on their phone and the sidebar is squished to almost nothing while the main content overflows sideways. Name two specific CSS habits from this module that would prevent this, and explain what each one actually does.
hints: One fix is about widths that don't adapt (fixed pixels vs max-width/relative). The other is about whether you tested at more than one size at all.
A media query is the tool for genuinely different layouts at different sizes, not just flexible widths.
explanation: Two real habits: (1) use max-width plus relative widths (width: 100%) instead of fixed pixel widths, so elements shrink to fit a narrower screen instead of forcing overflow; (2) add a media query (@media (max-width: ...)) to change the layout itself — like switching a flex row to flex-direction: column — below a certain screen width, rather than assuming the same side-by-side layout works at every size. Fixed widths and untested layouts are exactly what causes a page that looks right on one screen and breaks on another.

prompt: A stylesheet has both #main .highlight { color: orange; } and .highlight { color: purple; }, targeting the same element. Which color renders?

options.text: Orange — the id-containing selector is more specific, even combined with a class
Purple — .highlight alone is simpler, so it wins
It alternates between the two
Neither applies, since the selectors conflict

hints: A selector's specificity adds up across every part of it — an id anywhere in the chain raises the total significantly.
#main .highlight includes an id (#main) plus a class (.highlight) — compare that combined specificity to .highlight alone.
explanation: Orange. #main .highlight combines an id selector with a class selector, giving it higher total specificity than .highlight alone — even though the id (#main) isn't the element being colored directly, its presence in the selector chain still counts toward specificity. CSS doesn't average or alternate conflicting rules; specificity picks a single winner deterministically.

prompt: The page has <button class="save-btn">Save</button>. Which line correctly finds it with querySelector?

options.text: document.querySelector('.save-btn')
document.querySelector('save-btn')
document.querySelector('#save-btn')
document.querySelector(save-btn)

hints: A class selector needs the leading dot, the same as in a CSS stylesheet.
The element has class="save-btn", not id="save-btn" — the # prefix is for ids.
explanation: document.querySelector('.save-btn') — the leading dot signals "class," matching the element's class="save-btn". Without the dot, it looks for a <save-btn> tag, which doesn't exist. The # prefix looks for an id, which this element doesn't have. Unquoted, save-btn is read as a JavaScript expression (a subtraction of two variables named save and btn), not a selector string.

prompt: True or false: element.textContent = userTypedText is just as risky as element.innerHTML = userTypedText, since both are inserting text a user typed.

config.statement: textContent and innerHTML carry the same risk when inserting user-typed text.
config.rubric: A full answer says false and explains textContent always inserts plain, inert text while innerHTML parses its input as real HTML.

hints: One of these two parses its input as real markup. The other never does, regardless of what characters are in the string.
What would happen if userTypedText literally contained an HTML tag, for each of the two?
explanation: False. .innerHTML parses whatever string it's given as real HTML — a typed-in tag-like string can be interpreted as actual markup. .textContent inserts the exact same string as plain, inert text no matter what characters it contains — a literal shows up as visible text, not a real image tag. They look similar for ordinary text but behave very differently the moment the text contains anything tag-like.

prompt: Which correctly attaches a click handler to a button stored in the variable saveBtn?

options.text: saveBtn.addEventListener('click', function() { console.log('saved'); });
saveBtn.addEventListener(function() { console.log('saved'); });
saveBtn.onEvent('click', function() { console.log('saved'); });
saveBtn.click(function() { console.log('saved'); });

hints: addEventListener always needs the event type as its first argument, as a string.
There's no method called onEvent — the standard method is specifically named addEventListener.
explanation: saveBtn.addEventListener('click', function() {...}) — event type string first, then the callback. The second option omits the event type entirely. onEvent isn't a real method. .click(callback) doesn't attach a listener the way addEventListener does — .click() with no arguments actually simulates a click, which isn't the same thing at all.

prompt: Write the condition you'd check inside a keydown handler's callback to run code only when the Escape key was pressed, and explain where that information comes from.
hints: The callback automatically receives an event object as its first argument.
The specific key pressed is available as a property on that event object, as a string naming the key.
explanation: if (event.key === 'Escape') { ... } — the callback function passed to addEventListener automatically receives an event object (conventionally named event or e), and for a keydown event, event.key holds the string name of the specific key pressed ('Escape', 'Enter', 'a', etc.). Comparing it with === lets you run code only for that one key while the listener still catches every keypress in general.

options.text: An error
NaN

hints: input.value is always a string, regardless of the input's type attribute.
This is the exact "32" + 1 trap from earlier in the track — a string on the left of + joins as text.
explanation: "400100". input.value is always a string, even for a number-type input — so "400" + 100 joins as text rather than adding, producing "400100", not 500. The fix is the same as always: const total = Number(input.value) + 100; to convert deliberately before doing arithmetic.

prompt: Put these lines of a submit handler in the correct order.
hints: preventDefault() has to run before the browser's default reload happens — so it goes first inside the handler, not last.
You need the value read out before you can log it.
explanation: event.preventDefault() should run first, immediately inside the handler, to stop the reload before it happens — waiting until after other code runs risks the page reloading before your logic finishes. Then read and convert the value, then use it.

prompt: A panel needs to be genuinely hidden from both sighted users and screen readers when collapsed. Which CSS rule, toggled via classList, achieves that?

options.text: .hidden { display: none; }
.hidden { opacity: 0; }
.hidden { color: transparent; }
.hidden { font-size: 0; }

hints: opacity, color and font-size all only change appearance — the element is still fully present in the layout and still reachable.
Only one of these actually removes the element from the accessibility tree, not just from view.
explanation: display: none removes the element from both the visual layout and the accessibility tree — genuinely gone for everyone. opacity: 0, color: transparent, and font-size: 0 all only affect visual appearance; the element stays present and reachable by Tab and screen reader, which can leave someone focused on or hearing about something they can't see at all.

prompt: True or false: a toggle button that correctly shows/hides a panel with display: none has already done everything needed for a screen reader user, since the content really is hidden or shown correctly.

config.statement: Correctly toggling display: none is sufficient on its own — no further accessibility work is needed for the toggle button itself.
config.rubric: A full answer says false and explains that the button itself also needs aria-expanded (and ideally its own text) updated so its current state is announced.

hints: The panel being correctly hidden or shown is only half of the picture — what does the button itself communicate about its own state?
aria-expanded exists specifically to announce whether a toggle's associated content is currently expanded or collapsed.
explanation: False. Correctly hiding the panel with display: none means the panel's content is properly gone (or present) for everyone — but the button controlling it also needs to announce its own state, via aria-expanded (and ideally changed button text). Without that, a screen reader user knows the button exists but has no way to tell whether pressing it will show or hide the panel, or what its current state already is.

prompt: A developer wants a highly custom-shaped clickable element and considers <div class="fancy-btn" onclick="...">. What's the accessibility-preserving alternative that keeps the same visual freedom?

options.text: Use <button class="fancy-btn"> instead — CSS can restyle it however needed, while keeping free keyboard behavior
Add a CSS class named "accessible" to the div
There's no alternative — divs are required for fully custom shapes
Add an alt attribute to the div

hints: CSS has no real limitation that forces reaching for a div over a button for visual styling.
alt is an attribute for images, not a general accessibility fix for arbitrary elements.
explanation: <button class="fancy-btn"> keeps all the free keyboard behavior (Tab-reachable, Enter/Space-activatable) while allowing exactly the same CSS styling freedom a div would have — there's no visual constraint that actually requires a div here. A class named "accessible" does nothing on its own; alt applies to images, not buttons.

prompt: A developer removes a page's default focus outline with outline: none; because they thought it looked messy, and doesn't add any replacement. Explain concretely who this breaks, and what the fix should be.
hints: Think specifically about someone navigating the page with Tab, not a mouse — what do they currently rely on that outline for?
The fix isn't 'put outline: none back' necessarily — it's making sure some visible focus indicator always exists.
explanation: This breaks anyone navigating by keyboard: without a visible focus indicator, they can press Tab repeatedly and have no way to see which element currently has focus, making the whole page effectively unusable without a mouse even though every element might technically still be reachable. The fix isn't necessarily restoring the default outline — it's replacing it with a deliberate, visible focus style (a custom outline color, a background highlight) so focus is always visible, just not necessarily the default browser style if that's genuinely a design concern.

prompt: document.querySelector('#logBtn') returns null. What's the most likely cause?

options.text: No element on the page has id="logBtn" — likely a typo in the id or the selector
The page has too many elements for querySelector to search
querySelector always returns null the first time it's called
IDs can't be searched with querySelector

hints: null from querySelector always means 'nothing on the page matched this selector.'
Double-check both the selector string and the actual id attribute in the HTML for an exact match, including case.
explanation: null specifically means no element matched — almost always a mismatch between the selector and the actual HTML, like a typo in the id, a missing # in the selector, or the script running before that element exists in the page yet.

prompt: A button needs to run a function only on the second and later clicks, never the first. Which building block from this module makes that possible at all?

options.text: A variable outside the handler, tracking whether this is the first click, checked and updated inside the addEventListener callback
addEventListener has a built-in 'skip first click' option
This is impossible in JavaScript
Using two separate buttons

hints: The callback function runs fresh each time, but a variable declared outside it (in the surrounding scope) persists between calls.
There's no such built-in addEventListener option — this needs to be tracked manually.
explanation: A variable declared outside the callback (let hasClicked = false;) persists across every call, since the callback closes over it — check and update it inside the handler (if (hasClicked) { ... } hasClicked = true;). addEventListener itself has no built-in skip-first behavior; this state has to be tracked by hand.

prompt: A number input's value needs to be doubled and displayed. Which line correctly does the conversion and math together?

options.text: const doubled = Number(input.value) * 2;
const doubled = input.value * 2;
const doubled = input.value + input.value;
const doubled = String(input.value) * 2;

hints: input.value is a string — it needs to be explicitly converted before real arithmetic, not just multiplied directly.
Even though * happens to auto-convert numeric-looking strings, converting deliberately first is the clearer, safer habit this module has been building on.
explanation: Number(input.value) * 2 converts deliberately, on purpose, before doing arithmetic — the reliable habit from earlier in the track. input.value * 2 would actually still work here since * auto-converts a numeric string, but relying on that instead of converting explicitly is exactly the kind of "hoping an operator does it" habit this track has been steering away from. input.value + input.value joins as text if value is a string (doubling the digits as text, not the number). String(input.value) * 2 converts the wrong direction entirely.

prompt: A page has a form. Clicking Submit reloads the page every time, wiping out a status message the JavaScript was supposed to show. What single line, and where, fixes this?

options.text: event.preventDefault(); as the first line inside the submit handler
event.preventDefault(); as the last line inside the submit handler
form.reload = false; anywhere in the script
Removing the <form> tags entirely

hints: preventDefault() has to run before the browser's default reload actually kicks in — placement matters.
There's no reload property on a form element — that's not how this default behavior gets controlled.
explanation: event.preventDefault(); as the first line inside the handler — calling it early ensures the reload is cancelled before anything else runs, rather than risking the page reloading partway through your logic if it were called last or conditionally. form.reload isn't a real property; removing the <form> tags would lose the built-in form behaviors (like Enter-to-submit) rather than fixing anything.

prompt: Sort each way of hiding an element by whether it's also removed from the accessibility tree (genuinely gone for a screen reader) or only hidden visually.

items.text: color: transparent; (text made invisible, box still there)
Removing the element from the DOM entirely with JavaScript

hints: Anything that only changes appearance (opacity, color) leaves the element structurally present and reachable.
display: none and actually removing the element are the two approaches that take it out of the accessibility tree, not just out of view.
explanation: display: none and outright DOM removal both take the element out of the accessibility tree, not just out of sight. opacity: 0 and color: transparent both leave the element fully present and reachable by keyboard and screen reader — invisible to the eye, but not actually gone.

prompt: A toggle button's aria-expanded is set to "true" once, in the HTML, and never updated by JavaScript afterward even as the panel is repeatedly shown and hidden. What's the practical effect?

options.text: A screen reader announces "expanded" every time, regardless of the panel's actual current state
Nothing — aria-expanded only matters on page load
The panel stops toggling visually
The browser automatically keeps it in sync without JavaScript's help

hints: aria-expanded is just an attribute — nothing updates it automatically when other, unrelated code changes the panel's visibility.
The panel's visual toggle and the aria-expanded attribute are two separate things that both need to be kept in sync by your code.
explanation: A static aria-expanded="true" that's never updated will announce "expanded" forever, regardless of what's actually happening visually — actively wrong information is arguably worse than no aria-expanded at all. It has to be updated in the same event handler that toggles the panel's visibility, exactly like lesson 4 demonstrated, or the two states drift apart.

prompt: A "Delete entry" action is built as a <span> styled to look like a link, with an onclick handler, colored blue with an underline. List every problem with this from this module, and what would fix each one.
hints: Think about both what's missing (keyboard reachability) and what a real semantic element would give for free.
There's a real element built for exactly this — a clickable action with a specific label.
explanation: Problems: (1) a <span> isn't part of the default keyboard tab order, so it's unreachable without a mouse — fixed by using a real <button> or <a> instead; (2) even if reached somehow, a span doesn't respond to Enter/Space by default, so activating it by keyboard wouldn't work either, which the native element also solves for free; (3) styling it to merely look like a link with color and underline, without being a real interactive element, means a screen reader announces it as plain text, not as an actionable control. The fix throughout is the same: use <button>Delete entry</button> (styled however desired with CSS), which gets keyboard reachability, activation, and correct screen-reader announcement all for free.

prompt: A form field is required, and a script needs to prevent submission (staying on the page, showing a message) if it's left empty. Which combination of tools from this module does that?

options.text: A submit handler that checks input.value, and calls event.preventDefault() when the value is empty
Deleting the <form> tag so nothing can ever submit
Setting the input's color to red permanently
This can only be done with a server, never in the browser

hints: preventDefault() doesn't have to be unconditional — it can be called only when a check inside the handler fails.
This is fully doable client-side with exactly the tools covered in this module: reading .value and conditionally preventing default.
explanation: A submit handler reads input.value, and if it's empty (or otherwise invalid), calls event.preventDefault() to block the actual submission while showing feedback — the same preventDefault tool from lesson 3, used conditionally instead of unconditionally. This is a genuine client-side capability; a server-side check is still good practice for real security, but the immediate, before-any-network-request validation is exactly what preventDefault plus a value check gives you in the browser.

prompt: Which correctly saves the string "dark" under the key "theme", so it's still there after the browser is fully closed and reopened?

options.text: localStorage.setItem('theme', 'dark');
let theme = 'dark';
sessionStorage.setItem('theme', 'dark');
console.log('theme: dark');

hints: Only localStorage persists across a full browser restart, not just a page reload.
sessionStorage clears when the tab closes — it doesn't survive closing the whole browser.
explanation: localStorage.setItem('theme', 'dark') is the only option here that survives closing the browser entirely and reopening it. A plain variable is wiped on any reload. sessionStorage clears when its tab is closed, which is sooner than a full browser restart. console.log just prints to the console — it saves nothing at all.

prompt: localStorage.setItem('steps', 8000); is saved. Later: const total = localStorage.getItem('steps') + 2000; console.log(total); What actually prints, and what one change fixes it to print the real sum?
hints: getItem always returns a string, regardless of what type was originally saved.
The fix is the same Number(...) conversion used everywhere else in this track for this exact problem.
explanation: It prints "80002000" — getItem returns the string "8000", and + with a string on the left joins as text rather than adding. The fix: const total = Number(localStorage.getItem('steps')) + 2000; which converts the retrieved string to a real number before the arithmetic, correctly producing 10000.

prompt: You have const entry = { pain: 6, notes: 'tired' }; and want to save the full object to localStorage so it can be correctly loaded back later. Which line actually preserves the data?

options.text: localStorage.setItem('entry', JSON.stringify(entry));
localStorage.setItem('entry', entry);
localStorage.setItem('entry', entry.toString());
localStorage.entry = entry;

hints: Passing the object directly to setItem triggers a generic, data-losing string conversion, not a data-preserving one.
.toString() on a plain object also produces the unhelpful "[object Object]" text, same as the default conversion.
explanation: JSON.stringify(entry) converts the object into a real, data-preserving JSON string like '{"pain":6,"notes":"tired"}'. Passing the object directly, or calling .toString() on it, both trigger the generic "[object Object]" conversion, which discards the actual property values entirely.

prompt: Put these lines in the correct order to save an entry, then immediately load it back and read one of its fields.
hints: You need a real object before you can stringify it, and a saved string before you can parse it.
loaded.pain only works once loaded is a real object again, which requires JSON.parse to have already run.
explanation: Create the object, stringify and save it, read the saved string back, parse it into a real object, then access its field. Each line depends on the one before it — skipping or reordering any step (like trying to parse before getItem has run) would break the chain.

prompt: True or false: code that works correctly when you test it in your own browser is guaranteed to also work correctly for a first-time visitor with nothing saved yet.

config.statement: If storage code works in your own browser, it will work the same way for a brand-new visitor.
config.rubric: A full answer says false and explains that a developer's own browser usually already has leftover test data, hiding the null/first-visit case.

hints: What's usually sitting in your own browser's localStorage by the time you're testing a feature?
The null/first-visit case is exactly what's hidden by leftover data from earlier testing.
explanation: False. A developer's own browser almost always has leftover saved data from earlier testing, which silently hides the never-saved (null) case the entire time you're developing. A genuinely new visitor, with nothing saved, hits exactly the code path your own testing never exercised — which is precisely why this bug is so common and so easy to miss until a real new user hits it.

prompt: Which line safely loads a list of entries, defaulting to an empty array if nothing has been saved yet?

options.text: const entries = localStorage.getItem('entries') ? JSON.parse(localStorage.getItem('entries')) : [];
const entries = JSON.parse(localStorage.getItem('entries'));
const entries = localStorage.getItem('entries');
const entries = [];

hints: The correct answer needs to actually parse real saved data when it exists, not just always fall back to empty.
JSON.parse(null) alone doesn't crash, but using the result as an array afterward would — the null check needs to happen before relying on entries as a real array.
explanation: The conditional expression parses the real saved string when one exists, and falls back directly to [] when getItem returns null — covering both cases correctly. The second option crashes when nothing is saved. The third never parses the JSON at all, leaving entries as a raw string. The fourth ignores any real saved data entirely, always starting from empty even when there's something to load.

prompt: Sort each piece of data by whether it's reasonably safe to store in localStorage or genuinely risky, given that it's unencrypted and readable by anyone with device access.

items.text: An unsent draft of a public blog post
A full name paired with a private diagnosis history

hints: Ask: would it be a real problem if anyone with access to this device read this value right now, in plain text?
A preference or an already-public draft reveals little if read by someone else on the same device.
explanation: Font size and an unsent draft of something meant to become public are low-stakes if read by someone else on the device. A plaintext password and an identifiable private medical history are both genuinely sensitive — exposing either to anyone with device access is a real problem, and neither belongs in unencrypted client-side storage.

prompt: True or false: because localStorage persists across reloads and browser restarts, it's a safe place to keep the only copy of several months of tracked health data.

config.statement: localStorage persisting across restarts makes it a safe sole backup for months of important data.
config.rubric: A full answer says false and explains that localStorage can still be cleared by private browsing, manual clearing, or storage limits, so it isn't a guaranteed backup.

hints: Persisting across an ordinary reload and being a guaranteed, permanent backup are two different claims.
Think about private browsing, manually clearing site data, or a browser's own storage limits.
explanation: False. localStorage does survive ordinary reloads and restarts, but it's not a guaranteed backup — private/incognito browsing wipes it on close, users can manually clear site data, and browsers can enforce storage limits. For data that would genuinely matter if lost, a real backend save is needed as the durable copy, with localStorage at most a convenient cache on top of it.

prompt: localStorage contains the truncated string '{"pain":6,"no' under the key 'entry' (a save that was interrupted mid-write). What happens when JSON.parse('{"pain":6,"no') runs, unguarded?

options.text: It throws a SyntaxError, and an uncaught throw stops the rest of the script from running
It returns null quietly, and the rest of the script continues normally
It returns whatever partial data it can salvage, like { pain: 6 }
It returns the original string unchanged

hints: JSON.parse doesn't attempt partial recovery of a malformed string — it either fully succeeds or fails loudly.
An uncaught error halts execution at that point — unlike getItem returning null, which is a normal, non-throwing value.
explanation: It throws a real SyntaxError — JSON.parse either fully succeeds on valid JSON or fails loudly on invalid JSON, with no partial-recovery attempt. Left uncaught, that thrown error stops the rest of the script from running, which is why a corrupted save can crash an entire page, not just the one feature that was loading data.

prompt: Write a load function that combines both this module's safety patterns: falls back to an empty array when nothing's saved, and also falls back to an empty array (without crashing the page) if the saved string is corrupted. Explain in one sentence why both checks are needed, not just one.
hints: The null check and the try/catch are solving two genuinely different problems — nothing saved yet, versus something saved but broken.
Both problems produce a non-usable value, but in different ways: one is a clean null, the other is a thrown error.

prompt: A to-do app saves its list with localStorage.setItem('todos', todos); where todos is a real array. Loading it back with JSON.parse(localStorage.getItem('todos')) throws a SyntaxError immediately, every time, even on a fresh save. What's the bug?

options.text: The save never used JSON.stringify, so the saved value is "[object Object]"-style unparseable text, not real JSON
JSON.parse doesn't work on arrays
getItem is spelled wrong
localStorage only works with numbers

hints: Check the save step, not just the load step — was the array actually converted to a JSON string first?
A missing JSON.stringify on the way in is a very common cause of a JSON.parse failure on the way out.
explanation: The array was never passed through JSON.stringify before setItem — the saved value is the generic, non-JSON string conversion, which JSON.parse can't make sense of. The fix is on the save side: localStorage.setItem('todos', JSON.stringify(todos));. JSON.parse works fine on real arrays that were properly stringified first.

prompt: A habit tracker shows a blank, broken page for every single first-time visitor, but works fine for the developer. The load code is: const habits = JSON.parse(localStorage.getItem('habits')); habits.forEach(...). What's the most likely cause?

options.text: For a first-time visitor, getItem returns null, JSON.parse(null) returns null, and null.forEach(...) throws
forEach doesn't work the first time a page loads
The developer's browser has a different version of JavaScript
habits was never declared

hints: The developer's browser almost certainly has leftover saved data — a first-time visitor genuinely doesn't.
null.forEach is exactly the kind of crash caused by treating a null value as if it were a real array.
explanation: For a genuinely new visitor, getItem('habits') returns null (nothing's ever been saved), JSON.parse(null) itself returns null without throwing, but calling .forEach() on that null value throws immediately. The developer's own browser has leftover test data, which is exactly why it's easy to miss this until a real first-time visitor hits it.

prompt: A settings page stores a user's session token (used to keep them logged in to a real backend) in localStorage so it survives a page reload. Is this an acceptable use, given this module's rules?

options.text: It depends on the specifics — but any credential-like value in unencrypted client storage carries real risk on a shared or compromised device, and needs to be weighed deliberately, not assumed safe
Yes, always — anything needed to stay logged in belongs in localStorage
No, under no circumstances should any session-related data ever be stored client-side
It doesn't matter, since localStorage is encrypted automatically

hints: This module's rule isn't a flat 'never store credentials' — it's 'know exactly what you're exposing on a shared or stolen device, and weigh it deliberately.'
localStorage has zero built-in encryption — that part is not automatic and not optional.
explanation: This is a genuinely nuanced real-world case, and the honest answer isn't a flat yes or no: a session token in localStorage is readable by anyone with device access, same as anything else stored there, so the real question is whether that specific risk (a shared/stolen device exposing an active session) has been considered and accepted, versus reached for without thinking. localStorage has no automatic encryption — that's a hard fact, not a judgment call.

prompt: A journaling app's load function is: const entries = JSON.parse(localStorage.getItem('entries')); with no null check and no try/catch. List the two separate failure modes this is exposed to, and the one-line fix for each.
hints: One failure mode involves a first-time visitor. The other involves a saved value that exists but is broken.
The fixes are a null-safe conditional and a try/catch, from lessons 3 and 5.
explanation: Failure 1: a first-time visitor, where getItem returns null — JSON.parse(null) returns null without throwing, but using entries as an array afterward (like entries.length) crashes. Fix: const entries = saved ? JSON.parse(saved) : []; Failure 2: a corrupted (non-null) saved string, where JSON.parse itself throws a SyntaxError, crashing the whole script if uncaught. Fix: wrap the parse in try/catch, falling back to an empty array in the catch block. Both fixes are needed together, since they guard against two different causes.

prompt: A page saves a user's preferred font size as a number, then on the next load does fontSize + 2 to compute a "larger" preview size, getting a string-joined result like "142" instead of the number 16. What's the minimal fix?

options.text: Wrap the loaded value in Number(...) before doing the addition
Switch from localStorage to sessionStorage
Use JSON.stringify when saving the number instead of setItem directly
Change + to a different operator entirely

hints: This is the same 'getItem always returns a string' issue from lesson 1, not a stringify/parse problem.
JSON.stringify/parse are for objects and arrays — a single plain number doesn't need them to round-trip through setItem/getItem.
explanation: Number(loadedValue) + 2 fixes it — the loaded value is a string (localStorage always returns strings), and converting it explicitly before the addition avoids the text-joining behavior of +. Switching storage type doesn't change the string-only behavior. JSON.stringify isn't required for a single plain number with setItem/getItem — it's specifically for objects and arrays.

prompt: True or false: once try/catch is added around JSON.parse, the null-safe check from lesson 3 (saved ? JSON.parse(saved) : []) becomes unnecessary, since try/catch already handles errors.

config.statement: try/catch alone makes the earlier null-safe ternary check redundant.
config.rubric: A full answer says false and explains that JSON.parse(null) doesn't throw at all, so try/catch alone wouldn't catch the null case — the two checks guard against different failure modes.

hints: Does JSON.parse(null) actually throw an error, or does it return something quietly?
try/catch only catches things that throw — it has no effect on a value that's returned normally, even if that value turns out to be unhelpful.
explanation: False. JSON.parse(null) doesn't throw — it returns null quietly, without an error to catch. try/catch only protects against a corrupted, non-null string that fails to parse; it does nothing for the separate case of nothing having been saved at all. Both checks are needed, each covering a distinct failure mode.

prompt: Put these debugging steps in order for a storage bug report: "the app crashes when I open it on a computer I've never used it on before."

items: Reproduce it: open the app in a browser with no prior saved data for this site
Check what getItem returns in that state (most likely null)
Check whether the code assumes the returned value is always real, parseable data
Add a null-safe fallback (and try/catch, if parsing is involved) so the first-visit state loads without crashing

hints: Reproducing the exact reported condition comes before diagnosing why it happens.
The fix should come last, only once the actual cause (an unhandled null) is confirmed.
explanation: Reproduce the first-time-visitor condition, check what's actually returned (null), identify that the code doesn't handle that case, then add the fix. Jumping straight to a fix without confirming the actual cause risks patching the wrong thing.

prompt: True or false: writing code that visually scrapes numbers off another website's rendered page counts as "using that site's API."

config.statement: Scraping data from a website's visual page is the same thing as using its API.
config.rubric: A full answer says false and explains an API is a deliberately published, structured way to request data, while scraping reads a page built for human eyes and breaks when the layout changes.

hints: An API is deliberately published and documented for programs to use — is a regular webpage built with that in mind?
Scraping depends on a page's specific visual layout, which is free to change at any time without warning — an API's structure is a deliberate contract.
explanation: False. An API is a deliberate, published, structured way for programs to request data, documented and meant to be relied on. Scraping reads a page that was built for a human to look at — it works only as long as that page's visual layout happens to stay the same, and breaks the moment it changes, since nothing about the page was ever designed to be machine-readable.

prompt: An API publishes /users/{id} (one specific user's profile) and /users (a list of all users). A developer needs just one specific user's details and requests /users by mistake. What happens?

options.text: A real, valid response comes back — the full list of all users, not the one profile that was actually needed
The API returns an error, since this isn't the intended request
Both endpoints always return exactly the same data
The request is automatically redirected to /users/{id}

hints: Different endpoints exist because they're built to answer different questions — neither one knows what you actually meant.
This is the same lesson as the weather forecast example: a valid endpoint, just not the right one for the actual need.
explanation: A real, valid response comes back — the full user list — since /users is itself a completely valid, working endpoint, just not the one that answers this specific question. This is a silent mismatch, not an error: nothing about the response looks broken, it's simply not what was actually needed.

prompt: Which line correctly sends a request to 'https://api.example.com/quote'?

options.text: fetch('https://api.example.com/quote')
get('https://api.example.com/quote')
fetch(https://api.example.com/quote)
request.fetch('https://api.example.com/quote')

hints: fetch is the actual built-in browser function name for this — no other name works.
The URL needs to be a quoted string, the same as any other specific piece of text.
explanation: fetch('https://api.example.com/quote') — the correct built-in function name, with the URL as a quoted string. There's no built-in function called get or request.fetch for this purpose, and an unquoted URL isn't valid syntax at all.

prompt: Put these steps in the correct order to get real, usable data from a fetch call using .then().
hints: The response wrapper has to exist before .json() can be called on it.
The real parsed data only exists after .json()'s own promise resolves — which needs its own .then().
explanation: fetch(url) sends the request and returns a Promise resolving to the response wrapper; .then(response => response.json()) extracts and starts parsing the real body, itself returning another Promise; the second .then() receives the actual parsed data. Each step depends on the one before it having completed.

options.text: Pauses execution of this function at that line until the Promise resolves, then continues with the real value
Skips the line entirely if the request is slow
Makes the request run twice, to be safe
Has no real effect — it's optional decoration

hints: await is specifically what makes the next line wait for real data instead of running immediately against a still-pending Promise.
Without await, response would be a Promise object, not the real response — await is what unwraps it correctly, in order.
explanation: await pauses execution of that specific function at that exact line, until the Promise resolves — then the next line runs with the real, resolved value instead of the pending Promise. This is what lets async code read top-to-bottom like ordinary sequential code, while still correctly waiting for the network.

prompt: True or false: await can be used inside any regular function, as long as it eventually calls fetch somewhere inside it.

config.statement: await works inside any function, as long as that function calls fetch somewhere.
config.rubric: A full answer says false and explains await is only legal syntax inside a function explicitly declared with the async keyword.

hints: The requirement is about how the function itself is declared, not about what it happens to call inside its body.
async and await are a matched pair — one enables the other, specifically.
explanation: False. await is only legal syntax inside a function explicitly declared async function name() { ... } — calling fetch somewhere inside a function doesn't make await usable in it. A regular, non-async function containing a bare await throws a syntax error, regardless of what else is in its body.

prompt: A fetch call fails because the device has no network connection at all. Which block of code actually catches this?

options.text: try { const response = await fetch(url); ... } catch (error) { ... }
if (!response.ok) { ... }
if (response.status === 404) { ... }
Nothing catches this — it can't be handled

hints: response.ok and response.status checks only run against a response object that actually exists — which requires the request to have completed at all.
A total connection failure means fetch's Promise rejects outright — that's specifically what try/catch is for.
explanation: try/catch around the await fetch call is what catches a genuine connection failure — fetch's Promise rejects, and catch handles that rejection. response.ok and response.status checks require an actual response object to exist first, which never happens if the request fails outright before any response arrives.

prompt: A page's fetch code has try/catch but no response.ok check. A request to a mistyped endpoint returns a real HTTP 404. Explain exactly what happens in the code, and what line needs to be added to actually catch this case.
hints: fetch doesn't reject just because the server responded with an error status — walk through what actually happens step by step.
The missing check is a boolean on the response object itself, checked right after the response arrives and before .json() is called.
explanation: Nothing throws: fetch resolves normally (a real, complete response did come back), the try block runs all the way through without triggering catch, and response.json() likely parses whatever error body the server sent — which may not even have the expected fields, silently producing undefined values downstream. The fix is adding if (!response.ok) { /* handle it */ return; } right after the response arrives, before calling .json(), so a 404 (or any other HTTP error status) is caught and handled explicitly instead of silently flowing through as if it were a successful response.

prompt: A developer hardcodes a paid API's key into their frontend JavaScript, then minifies the file before deploying, believing this keeps the key reasonably hidden. Is this reasoning correct?

options.text: No — minifying makes the code harder to read casually, but the full file (key included) is still downloaded to every visitor's browser and can be reformatted back to readable text in seconds
Yes — minified code cannot be reversed back into readable form
Yes — minifying encrypts the file's contents
It doesn't matter either way, since API keys can't be misused

hints: Minification changes formatting and variable names — it doesn't remove or encrypt any actual content, including the key.
Every byte of a minified file is still fully downloaded to the browser, just less pleasantly formatted.
explanation: No, the reasoning is incorrect. Minification only changes formatting for file-size and readability reasons — it isn't encryption, and it doesn't remove the key from the file. The full file, key included, is downloaded to every visitor's browser regardless, and un-minifying ("beautifying") a file back into readable form takes seconds with any standard tool.

prompt: Explain, in your own words, what a server-side proxy actually does to keep an API key secret, and why the browser itself can never be the place that holds the secret.
hints: Think about who makes the actual request to the third-party API in this setup, and who the browser talks to instead.
The key rule is: anything downloaded to a browser is downloaded, in full, to that browser — no code running there can keep a secret from the person using it.
explanation: A server-side proxy is a small server you control that holds the API key privately — the key never gets sent to any browser at all. The browser calls your own server instead of the third-party API directly; your server then makes the real API request (attaching the key itself), and passes just the resulting data back to the browser. The browser genuinely never sees the key. This has to work this way because anything shipped as frontend JavaScript is, by definition, downloaded in full to the browser running it — there's no code you can write that runs in a browser while keeping something hidden from that same browser.

prompt: console.log(fetch(url)) is run. What actually prints?

options.text: A Promise object, not the real data — fetch returns immediately, before the network request has completed
The real response data, since fetch waits for the network automatically
undefined, always
An error, since fetch requires await

hints: fetch never waits on its own — it returns immediately with something representing the eventual result.
await isn't required syntactically to call fetch, only to pause and unwrap what it returns.
explanation: A Promise object prints — fetch() returns immediately, without waiting for the network round trip to complete, handing back a placeholder representing the eventual result. Calling fetch without await isn't a syntax error; it just means you get the Promise itself rather than the resolved data.

prompt: A page fetches a quote API and displays quote data correctly most of the time, but shows "undefined" whenever the API happens to return zero quotes for a search with no matches. What's missing?

options.text: A check for a genuinely empty result, showing a real "no results" message instead of assuming data always exists
A try/catch block
A response.ok check
An async keyword

hints: This is a completely successful request and response — the server didn't fail, it correctly reported zero matches.
try/catch and response.ok both handle failure, not a valid response that just happens to contain no results.
explanation: This isn't a network failure or an HTTP error — it's a successful response that legitimately contains zero results. The fix is checking the parsed data itself (an empty array, for instance) and showing a real "No results found" message, rather than assuming there's always at least one item to display and blindly reading a property off of nothing.

prompt: A developer wraps their whole fetch call in try/catch, tests it by turning off WiFi entirely, and confirms the catch block correctly shows an error message. Have they fully tested the failure handling for this feature?

options.text: No — this only tests total network failure; a valid response with an HTTP error status (like 404 or 500) needs to be tested separately, since try/catch alone doesn't catch that
Yes — try/catch is a complete solution for every kind of fetch failure
No — try/catch doesn't actually work for testing purposes at all
Yes, as long as the WiFi test passed, nothing else can go wrong

hints: This module covered two genuinely separate failure modes — this test only exercises one of them.
A response.ok check needs its own deliberate test, like requesting a URL known to return a 404.
explanation: No — turning off WiFi only tests total network failure (caught by try/catch). A completed response reporting an HTTP error status, like a 404 from a mistyped endpoint, is a separate failure mode that try/catch alone doesn't catch — it needs its own explicit test, deliberately requesting a URL expected to return an error status, and confirming the response.ok check handles it.

prompt: Put these lines of a fully defensive fetch function in the correct order.
hints: The response.ok check has to happen after the response exists but before .json() is called on it.
The catch block needs to wrap everything that could throw, so it belongs at the end of the try block, not interspersed inside it.
explanation: Declare the async function, open try, await the fetch, check response.ok before attempting to parse the body, parse and use the data if the check passes, then close with catch to handle any genuine network failure that occurred anywhere inside the try block. Both failure modes — bad HTTP status and total network failure — are handled, each with its own distinct path.

prompt: A loading spinner is shown right before a fetch call starts, but the code only ever hides it inside the successful path, never inside catch. What happens on a genuine network failure?

options.text: The spinner stays visible forever, even though the error message is also shown underneath it
The spinner automatically disappears after a few seconds regardless
The catch block automatically hides any visible spinner without being told to
The page reloads automatically

hints: Nothing hides UI elements automatically just because an error occurred — every visual change has to be written explicitly.
The fix is hiding the spinner in both the success path and the catch block — or better, in one place that runs regardless of outcome.
explanation: The spinner stays visible forever, stuck on top of (or alongside) whatever error message does get shown, because nothing in the catch block was ever told to hide it — hiding it was only written into the success path. The fix is hiding the loading indicator in both places, or better, in a single place that always runs regardless of whether the request succeeded or failed.

prompt: True or false: a free, no-signup public API with no key at all has effectively zero client-side security considerations to think about.

config.statement: A free public API with no key has no security considerations worth thinking about at all.
config.rubric: A full answer says false — while there's no key to expose, other real-world concerns (rate limits, trusting the API's own reliability, and not sending unrelated sensitive data to it) can still matter.

hints: No key to expose is genuinely one real risk removed — but is it the only consideration that ever exists around calling a third-party service?
Think about what else might matter: reliability, rate limits, or what other data might accidentally be sent along with a request.
explanation: False, though this is a real nuance — a keyless public API does remove the specific key-exposure risk from lesson 5. But other considerations can still apply: the API's own uptime and rate limits affect your page's reliability, and it's still worth being deliberate about what data (if any) gets sent to a third party in the request itself. "No key" removes one specific risk; it doesn't mean there's nothing left to think about.

prompt: Describe, end to end, everything that should happen on a page from the moment a fetch call starts to the moment real data is shown — including every failure branch covered in this module. Don't write code, just describe the sequence of states.
hints: There are four real outcomes to account for: loading, success with data, success with an empty result, and failure (of two different kinds).
Make sure the loading state is guaranteed to end in every one of those outcomes, not just the successful one.
explanation: 1) Show a loading state the moment the request starts. 2) Await the fetch. 3a) If it throws (genuine network failure), catch it, hide the loading state, and show an honest network-error message. 3b) If it resolves but response.ok is false (an HTTP error status), hide the loading state and show a distinct server-error message. 3c) If it resolves successfully, parse the JSON body; if the resulting data is genuinely empty, hide the loading state and show a "no results" message. 3d) If it resolves successfully with real data, hide the loading state and display that data. Every one of these four end states has to explicitly turn off the loading indicator — that's the detail most likely to get missed.
